meaning.text: The word solovei generally means a nightingale, but it was also the name of a mythical hero, a robber.
Afanasyev says the name Nightingale was given on the basis of the ancient likening of the whistle of the storm to the thunderous song of this bird.
Afanasyev explains the epithet 'robber' by the destructive properties of the storm and by the old view that joined a robbing, thieving character to the personifications of clouds.

peoples_regions.region: the old epic tale of Ilya Muromets and Solovei-razboinik, whose hero's name is the most popular among the Russian people (въ русскомъ народѣ)
a Ukrainian tale (въ украинской сказкѣ) printed in 'Записки о южной Руси'

scene.text: He holds the straight road to Kiev, on which for thirty years no man walked, no beast ran and no bird flew.
He sits in a nest he has built on twelve (or nine) oaks.
His whistle is heard ten versts away.
At his whistle the dark forests bow down to the earth and the mother-river Smorodina is muddied with sand.

behavior_habitat.text: He blocked the straight road to Kiev for exactly thirty years, the time the bogatyr Ilya Muromets sat unable to move.
Sitting in his nest, he whistled so strongly and loudly that he threw everything down with his whistling, as if by the rush of a swift whirlwind.
When his whistle sounded, the bogatyr's horse under Ilya stumbled.
Brought to Prince Vladimir's court in Kiev and told to whistle at half-whistle, he answered that his lips were caked with blood and asked for a drink.
He took a cup of green wine weighing a bucket and a half in one hand and drank it in a single breath, then drank a second cup of beer and a third of sweet mead.
Having gathered great strength from the drink, he whistled and stunned the mighty bogatyrs so that they fell to the ground, while the common people fell dead.
His whistle shook the strong vaults of the prince's palace: the roof and turrets flew off and the iron ties burst.
He whistled like a nightingale, hissed like a serpent and roared like a beast (in a variant, like an aurochs).
His voice or whistle had the power of killing those who heard it.
Countless golden treasure lay in his cellars.
According to the bylina, his children turn into ravens with iron beaks.
His children turn into black ravens with iron noses.
His daughter, wishing to kill Ilya Muromets, threw a heavy gate-board down on him, but Ilya remained unharmed.
At his whistle walls and people fell.
He sits upon a tree, as does the div of the Lay of Igor's Campaign.

dealing_with_it.text: The bogatyr Ilya Muromets knocked him down from the high oaks with a tempered arrow and carried him with him to Kiev.
Angered, Ilya Muromets killed him by throwing him, according to one variant, higher than the standing tree and a little lower than the walking cloud.

origin.text: Afanasyev concludes that in the figure of Solovei-razboinik the popular fantasy personified the demon of the stormy thundercloud.

Afanasyev says the tale of Solovei-razboinik, nesting on high oaks, arose from the same source as the name of Perun's speaking bird: the likening of thunder and the howl of the storm to speech and song.

rationale.text: Afanasyev retells and quotes the bylina of Ilya Muromets and Solovei-razboinik, which he introduces with the remark that Ilya's name is the most popular among the Russian people.
Afanasyev reports a Ukrainian tale, printed in 'Записки о южной Руси', in which Solovei-razboinik takes the place of Zmey Gorynych.
Ralston's footnote names Solovei as a mythical robber whose voice or whistle killed those who heard it, and on that passage does not cite or quote Afanasyev, so it counts as an independent source.

Afanasyev's three volumes count as one source; with Ralston that is two independent authors and two peoples, the minimum for widely-attested, and the Ukrainians row rests on a single sentence of Afanasyev's.

notes.text: appearance: no source describes his body, size, dress or form; searched solovei, Solovei, solovei razboinik, nightingale, nightingale robber, robber, соловей, разбойник, соловей-разбойник, соловей разбойник, соловья-разбойник, соловье-разбойник, соловью-разбойник, соловья разбой in all sources. The only bodily detail met is his own remark at Vladimir's court that his lips were caked with blood (afanasyev1865:p.306), kept under behavior_habitat as an event rather than drawn as a description. The scene field carries the sourced setting.

variants: no source describes him differently by people or region. Afanasyev reports only that in one Ukrainian tale Solovei-razboinik takes the place of Zmey Gorynych (afanasyev1865:p.307), which is recorded under peoples_regions and related.

Every narrative clause comes from Afanasyev's retelling and quotation of the bylina of Ilya Muromets (afanasyev1865:pp.306-309) and his asides elsewhere. The meaning clauses from afanasyev1865:pp.308-309 and both origin clauses are Afanasyev's own mythological interpretation (a storm-cloud demon), not peasant belief, and are hedged as his. Ralston (ralston1873:p.258) gives only a footnote.

The Russians row rests on afanasyev1865:p.302, where Afanasyev introduces the old epic tale of Ilya Muromets and Solovei-razboinik and says Ilya's name is the most popular among the Russian people; the page ties the epic, not Solovei by name, to that people, and the native rows' people follows the same reading (the variant Solovei also rests on Ralston's Russian Folk-Tales footnote). The verify agent should judge whether that is narrow enough.

afanasyev1868:p.526 compares Solovei's wall-felling whistle with the whistle of the fiery serpent and the roar of Tugarin; that comparison is Afanasyev's, so no related link to tugarin was made. afanasyev1868:p.709 compares another bogatyr's blowing with Solovei's whistle and was not used.

Verify judgment on the Russians row: kept and flagged. afanasyev1865:p.302 opens Afanasyev's discussion of the epic of Ilya Muromets and Solovei-razboinik and ties Ilya's name, in songs and traditions, to the Russian people; it does not name the people for Solovei himself. The two native rows' people rests on the same passage context, since their cited pages (pp.306-307) print the forms but no people term.
